catalog_quote: [François 2005:451] The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). Exactly the same evolution is attested in modern French: due to the progressive loss of all etymological posttonic vowels, French has become a perfectly oxytone language. [p. 468] A similar pattern is also represented by Vurës, with its diphthong /ia/ already illustrated in (15) and (16). It only surfaces as [ia] under primary stress, whereas it takes the form of a monophthong [i] in all other contexts: (32) Correspondence between stressed [ia] and unstressed [i] in Vurës: PNCV *tabe ‘love, honor’ → *tabe-tabe > timtiam ‘loving’ ... PNCV *mwera ‘child’ → *mwera-mwera > ŋmwirŋmwiar ‘children’ [Malau 2016 §2.5, Google Books snippet] 2.5 Stress Vurës has fixed word stress, falling on the final syllable of the word. There are no exceptions to this stress placement rule in native words. However, whilst in some cases borrowings take on Vurës stress placement, in other instances the stress placement of the word in the donor language is retained. Below are some examples of disyllabic and trisyllabic words in Vurës, indicating variable syllable structure and consistent final syllable stress.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (HAL halshs-00524988, 63 pp., text present; extracted text, no scanned). p. 10 = printed p. 451, §3.1 'Prosodic stress and vowel reduction': the passage is there verbatim except that the text renders 'fi' as '²' ("word-²nal posttonic vowels.. stressed on their ²nal rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). Exactly the same evolution is attested in modern French.. French has become a perfectly oxytone language."); the compilers silently restored 'final', as flagged in its exceptions entry. p. 27 = printed p. 468, §5.1.2.2, ex. (32): "A similar pattern is also represented by Vurës, with its diphthong /ia/ already illustrated in (15)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the final syllable of the word (the language is oxytone), as in all the Banks–Torres languages surveyed, Vurës included; the Vurës-specific evidence given is that the diphthong /ia/ appears as [ia] only under primary stress, i.e. in the final syllable of forms like timtiam, mwikmwiak, mwirmwiar, and reduces to [i] elsewhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for modern Vurës; the article only reconstructs secondary stress on every second syllable leftward of the penult in the pre-reduction protoforms (p. 451).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Vurës. The only exception noted in the area is Dorig, where a word-internal long /aː/ attracts stress (p. 468). The PDF text renders 'fi' as '²' (font artifact); the quote above restores 'final'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical words in isolation, historical-comparative framing). The statement is an areal generalization over all 17 Banks/Torres languages based on the author's own fieldwork (Vurës collected May–July 1998, fn. 2 p. 443, supplemented by Hyslop n.d. b); it is not a sentence from a Vurës-dedicated description. The primary description, Malau 2016 ch. 2 (pp. 19–48), could not be opened and should supersede this once obtained.
new_statements.identity_note: Vurës proper (vure1239 / msn), west-central Vanua Lava. No dialect is named in François 2005; his Vurës data come from his own 1998 survey plus Hyslop (Malau) n.d., i.e. the same variety documented in Malau 2016/2021 (Vetuboso area community). Not to be confused with Vera'a (vera1241) or Mwesen (mose1250), the neighbouring Vanua Lava languages also covered by François's areal statement.
